extracted.intended_audience: researchers/authors reporting in vivo animal studies (and journal editors/reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors on how to report animal experiments to ensure ethical oversight, transparent methods (housing, husbandry, analgesia, monitoring), interpretation, limitations, and generalisability/translation of findings. Intended to improve reproducibility, welfare reporting and enable appropriate evaluation by editors and reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the name of the ethical review committee or equivalent that has approved the use of animals in this study and any relevant licence or protocol numbers (if applicable). If ethical approval was not sought or granted, provide a justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must comply with regulations and guidelines for animal use and obtain relevant approval from an appropriate ethics committee/regulatory body before starting work. Provide a clear statement explaining how the study conforms to appropriate regulations and guidelines, include the institution where research was approved, the ethics committee (e.g. IACUC, AWERB) and indicate protocol or project licence numbers so the study can be identified. Also add relevant accreditation (e.g. AAALAC, GLP). If formal ethical approval was not required (e.g. species/practice not covered by regulation), demonstrate compliance with international standards, cite the reference, and explain why the research is exempt. Examples provided show model phrasing including licence numbers and institutional committee names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Housing and husbandry
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide details of housing and husbandry conditions, including any environmental enrichment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report housing/husbandry because environment affects animal health, behaviour and experimental outcomes. Consider reporting: cage/tank/housing system (type and dimensions); food and water (type, composition, supplier, access); bedding and nesting material; temperature and humidity; sanitation (frequency of cage/tank water changes, material transfer, water quality); social environment (group size/composition/stocking density); biosecurity; lighting (type, schedule, intensity); environmental enrichment (structural enrichment, species-typical resources, toys, exercise opportunities, novelty). Also report sex of experimenter if relevant. If no enrichment was provided, state this with justification; likewise provide scientific justification for withholding food/water or singly housing animals. If space is limited, include details via a public repository or supplementary information. The guidance includes many references and concrete examples of how these factors affect physiology and behaviour, and sample 'example' paragraphs showing full reporting of husbandry details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal care and monitoring — pain/suffering mitigation (16a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe any interventions or steps taken in the experimental protocols to reduce pain, suffering, and distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a thorough description of pain management strategies because untreated pain affects biology and variability. Clearly describe: the specific analgesic(s); administration method (formulation, route, dose, concentration, volume, frequency, timing, and equipment used); rationale for choice (model, disease/pathology, procedure, mechanism, pharmacokinetics, personnel safety); protocol modifications to reduce pain/distress (changes to anaesthetic protocol, increased monitoring, habituation, procedural modifications). If analgesics or reasonable welfare measures were withheld for experimental reasons, report the scientific justification. Examples include specific dosing regimens, voluntary ingestion methods, and analgesia-based decision trees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal care and monitoring — adverse events (16b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report any expected or unexpected adverse events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report adverse events that negatively impacted animal welfare (e.g. cardio/respiratory depression, CNS disturbance, hypothermia, reduced food intake), and indicate whether they were expected or unexpected. If none were observed or recorded, explicitly state this. Reporting adverse events helps other researchers plan welfare assessments and informs risk–benefit evaluations for interventions. Examples illustrate how to log events, criteria used to define illness, and how events informed protocol changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal care and monitoring — humane endpoints and monitoring frequency (16c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the humane endpoints established for the study, the signs that were monitored, and the frequency of monitoring. If the study did not have humane endpoints, state this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define humane endpoints (predetermined morphological, physiological and/or behavioural signs triggering removal from study) and report them for the specific species/strain. Include clear criteria of clinical signs monitored and signs that led to euthanasia or other actions (general welfare indicators: weight loss, reduced food intake, abnormal posture; procedure-specific indicators: tumour size, sensory-motor deficits). Report timing and frequency of monitoring, considering circadian rhythms and critical periods (post-surgery, disease progression, following adverse events). Publishing score sheets of monitored signs is encouraged to guide others. Report this information even if no animals reached endpoints; if none were established, explicitly state so. Examples show monitoring schedules, scoring thresholds and actions taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation / scientific implications (17a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret the results, taking into account the study objectives and hypotheses, current theory, and other relevant studies in the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret results in the context of study objectives (see objectives item). For hypothesis-testing studies, restrict interpretations to the primary outcome; exploratory outcomes should not be described as conclusive. Discuss findings relative to current theory and preferably reference relevant systematic reviews; avoid selectively citing only supporting or statistically significant studies. Where appropriate, describe implications for improving welfare or reducing animal numbers (e.g. methods that reduce variance and thus sample sizes). Examples illustrate contrasting data interpretations and possible reductions in animal use from methodological improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment on study limitations including bias and model limitations (17b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment on the study limitations including potential sources of bias, limitations of the animal model, and imprecision associated with the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss unavoidable limitations to place findings in context and to guide future work. Describe the quality of evidence and appropriateness of the animal model for the research question. Address internal validity and whether potential risks of bias were mitigated — specifically refer to sample size, inclusion/exclusion criteria, randomisation, and blinding. Be transparent about extrapolation limits and mechanistic uncertainties. Examples demonstrate candid descriptions of model limitations and potential unaddressed confounders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalisability / translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment on whether, and how, the findings of this study are likely to generalise to other species or experimental conditions, including any relevance to human biology (where appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the type of study (hypothesis-testing vs exploratory) when assessing generalisability. Discuss what further research is required to support generalisation or translation (e.g. different species, additional experiments). Interpret results in relation to current evidence, and discuss factors that may moderate effects (population: age, sex, strain, species; intervention: different drugs of same class; outcome: different assessment approaches). Thoughtful discussion prevents unnecessary/ unethical follow-up studies and better informs translational decisions. Examples and references are provided to guide appropriate scope of claims.
